title: What the sea gave
hook: the treasures rise, and people read them two ways
carry: one story, read as holy event and inner path
tomorrow: the nectar's finally out, and everyone grabs. who gets a taste?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the poison that came first: Shiva swallowed it so the world could live, his throat turned blue, and the work still held. Now a cow, a horse and a goddess rise from the sea. Real, or a picture?

Kamadhenu, a cow that grants wishes. A white horse. Airavata, a white elephant. A tree in flower. The moon. A great jewel. Then, standing on a lotus, Lakshmi, the goddess of fortune, who chooses Vishnu. Last of all comes Dhanvantari, the physician of the gods, carrying the pot of amrita. It reads like the end of a long quest when the loot finally drops. And people who love this story have a real argument about it: did this happen, or is it a picture of something inside you?
screen: `THE SEA STARTS GIVING.` → `LAKSHMI ON A LOTUS.` → `DID IT HAPPEN, OR IS IT YOU?`

segments.voice: The Puranas list the treasures a little differently, but the shape is the same: the sea gives, once the poison is behind it. And the treasures are still on the calendar: Dhanteras, two days before Diwali, honors Dhanvantari rising with the amrita, and on Diwali night families worship Lakshmi. Now the two readings, each at its best. The first: these are holy events. Vishnu really came down as the tortoise; Lakshmi really rose from the sea; the amrita is real. For devotees who hold this, the story isn't a code to crack. It's the history of the gods, and part of why Lakshmi is worshipped and Vishnu trusted to hold the world. Turning it into a metaphor, this side says, shrinks the gods to fit inside your head. The second: the churning is a picture of the inner life. Some teachers read the ocean as the mind, the churning as long practice, the poison as the hard stuff that surfaces first, and the nectar as freedom at the end. On this reading the story belongs to anyone who has worked through something hard. Keeping it only as events, this side says, leaves it on a shelf. Hindu tradition doesn't make you choose: one story can be holy history and an inner path at once, and many pray to Lakshmi and also hear the churning as their own story. Both readings agree on the order: poison first, treasures after.
screen: `THE SEA GIVES ITS TREASURES.` · `DHANTERAS AND DIWALI.` · `READING ONE: HOLY EVENTS.` · `READING TWO: THE INNER CHURNING.` · then, large: `ONE STORY, BOTH AT ONCE.`

segments.voice: Pick up or look at one object near you: a ring, a mug, a photo. For the first half of the sit, see it only as a thing, its weight, its color, its edges. For the second half, let it be what it stands for: who gave it, what it holds for you. If you pray, you can give thanks to God for both.
Kurma: the tortoise underneath the churning, while the treasures rise into the light.
